updates.text: Which statements best characterize the focus of physical metallurgy?

statements.text: It studies physical and mechanical characteristics of metals and alloys.
It examines how composition, mechanical processing and heat treatment influence those characteristics.
Microstructure–property relationships are central to the subject.
After heat treatment, property changes are attributed mainly to changes in bulk composition; microstructure and defect structure are secondary.

updates.keyExplanation: Statements 1–3 describe the scope of physical metallurgy. Statement 4 is incorrect because heat treatment commonly changes phase distribution, grain structure, precipitates and defect populations without changing the alloy's bulk composition.
updates.concise: Physical metallurgy links composition and processing to microstructure and properties; heat treatment need not change bulk composition.
updates.detailed: Physical metallurgy investigates how processing and composition create microstructures that control material properties. A heat treatment can change phases, grain size, precipitate distribution and dislocation density while leaving the nominal bulk composition essentially unchanged. Therefore statement 4 reverses the usual microstructure-based explanation.

updates.text: Which statements correctly distinguish metallic bonding from covalent bonding?

statements.text: Metallic bonding uses delocalised valence electrons, whereas covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs localised between bonded atoms.
Metallic bonding is generally non-directional, whereas covalent bonding is directional.

updates.keyExplanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are broadly correct for the introductory comparison. Statement 3 is false because metallic and covalent bond energies overlap substantially; metallic bonding is not universally an order of magnitude weaker.
updates.concise: Metallic bonding is delocalised and non-directional; covalent bonding is directional. Their bond energies are not separated by a universal tenfold ratio.
updates.detailed: Metallic bonding is described using delocalised valence electrons and is generally non-directional, helping explain the plasticity of many metals. Covalent bonds are directional; covalent network solids such as diamond are often brittle. Bond-energy ranges overlap, so one cannot claim that metallic bonds are always at least ten times weaker than covalent bonds.

statements.text: A deeper well generally indicates stronger cohesive bonding and a higher melting temperature.

updates.keyExplanation: Both statements are true in their qualified form. Grain refinement raises yield strength by impeding slip transfer and can improve resistance to cleavage, but its effect on toughness is not guaranteed for every alloy or loading condition.
updates.concise: Grain refinement often gives a favorable strength–toughness balance, but no strengthening mechanism has a universal toughness outcome.
updates.detailed: Smaller grains increase the number of boundaries that can impede dislocation motion, raising yield strength through the Hall–Petch effect over its normal range. Refinement can also reduce the size of cleavage facets and improve brittle-fracture resistance. These trends depend on chemistry, phase structure, temperature and fracture mode, so grain refinement should not be described as the only mechanism that can improve both strength and toughness in all cases.
